title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter III
paragraphs:
“Say, goddess, what ensued, when Raphael,
The affable archangel . . .
Eve
The story heard attentive, and was filled
With admiration, and deep muse, to hear
Of things so high and strange.”
—_Paradise Lost_, B. vii.

If Mr. Casaubon really had begun to consider Miss Brooke a suitable wife, the reasons that could persuade her to accept him were already planted in her mind. By the following evening they had budded and blossomed. That morning they had talked at length, while Celia, who did not enjoy the company of Mr. Casaubon’s moles and yellow complexion, escaped to the vicarage to play with the curate’s cheerful, poorly shod children.

By now Dorothea had gazed deep into the unmeasured reservoir of Mr. Casaubon’s mind. There she saw every quality she herself possessed reflected back in vague, labyrinthine expanses. She had shared much of her own experience with him and learned the scope of his great work, which also stretched into an enticing labyrinth. He had instructed her like Milton’s “affable archangel,” and with something of that angel’s manner explained his undertaking. He would show that every system of myth, every stray fragment of myth in the world, was a corrupted form of an originally revealed tradition. Others had attempted this before, admittedly, but without the thoroughness, fairness of comparison and effective arrangement he intended. Once one had grasped the true position and stood firmly upon it, the vast field of mythological structures became intelligible—indeed, shone with the reflected light of their correspondences. Gathering that great harvest of truth, however, was neither quick nor easy. His notes already filled a formidable row of volumes. The crowning labour would be to compress these abundant and still accumulating findings so that, like the earlier harvest of Hippocratic books, they fitted on one small shelf. Mr. Casaubon explained all this to Dorothea much as he would to a fellow scholar: he did not command two different styles of conversation. True, whenever he used Greek or Latin he scrupulously supplied the English, but he would probably have done that in any company. A learned country clergyman habitually thinks of his acquaintances as “lords, knights, and other noble and worthy men, who know but little Latin.”

The breadth of this conception utterly captivated Dorothea. Here was something beyond the shallows of schoolroom literature for young ladies. Here was a living Bossuet, whose work would bring complete knowledge into harmony with devoted faith; a modern Augustine, combining the glories of learned doctor and saint.

His holiness seemed as evident as his learning. Dorothea felt moved to speak openly about subjects she could discuss with nobody she had previously met at Tipton. In particular, she spoke of how church forms and statements of belief mattered less than spiritual religion: the surrender of self in communion with Divine perfection which she found expressed in the finest Christian books of widely separated ages. Mr. Casaubon understood her immediately. He assured her that he shared this view, when properly moderated by wise conformity, and could cite historical examples she had never heard of.

“He thinks as I do,” Dorothea told herself, “or rather, his thought contains a whole world of which mine is only a cheap little mirror. And his feelings, his entire experience—what a lake beside my tiny pool!”

Miss Brooke drew conclusions from words and inclinations as readily as any girl her age. Signs are small and measurable; interpretations have no limit. In sweet, passionate girls, any sign may summon wonder, hope and belief as vast as the sky, coloured by the diffusion of a thimbleful of knowledge. They are not always very badly deceived. Even Sinbad may by chance have given a true account, and faulty reasoning sometimes brings poor mortals to correct conclusions. Starting far from the right point, then travelling in loops and zigzags, we occasionally reach exactly where we ought to be. Miss Brooke’s haste in trusting therefore does not prove Mr. Casaubon unworthy of her trust.

He stayed a little longer than planned, yielding to mild pressure from Mr. Brooke, whose only inducement was his own collection of documents about machine-breaking and hayrick-burning. Summoned to the library, Mr. Casaubon faced a heap of them while his host picked up first one and then another to read aloud. His reading wandered and faltered, jumping from one unfinished passage to the next with a “Yes, now, but here!” Finally he pushed the whole pile aside and opened the diary of his youthful travels on the Continent.

“Look here—this is all about Greece. Rhamnus, the ruins of Rhamnus—you’re a great Greek scholar, now. I don’t know whether you’ve studied the topography much. I spent no end of time working these things out—Helicon, for instance. Here, now! ‘Next morning we set out for Parnassus, the twin-peaked Parnassus.’ This whole volume is about Greece, you know,” Mr. Brooke concluded, running his thumb across the edges of the pages as he held the book out.

Mr. Casaubon formed a dignified, if rather sorrowful, audience. He bowed at the right moments and, so far as he could without appearing impatient or dismissive, avoided examining any documents. He remembered that this haphazardness was connected with the country’s institutions, and that the man driving him through this punishing mental scramble was not merely a kindly host but a landowner and custos rotulorum, keeper of the county records. Did the thought that Mr. Brooke was Dorothea’s uncle also help him endure it?

He certainly seemed increasingly intent on getting her to talk to him, on drawing her out, as Celia privately observed. When he looked at her, a smile often lit his face like pale winter sunshine. Before leaving the next morning, during a pleasant walk with Miss Brooke along the gravel terrace, he mentioned the drawbacks of his solitary life. He felt the need for that cheerful companionship through which youth’s presence can lighten or vary the serious labours of maturity. He delivered this statement as precisely and carefully as a diplomatic envoy whose words were expected to have consequences. Indeed, Mr. Casaubon did not generally expect to repeat or revise anything he said about practical or personal matters. An inclination deliberately stated on the second of October should, he thought, need only a reference to that date. He judged by his own memory, a volume in which a vide supra—a “see above”—could replace repetition, rather than the ordinary, much-used blotting book bearing only traces of forgotten writing. In this instance, however, his confidence was unlikely to prove misplaced. Dorothea heard and remembered his words with the eager interest of a fresh young nature for which every new kind of experience marks an epoch.

It was three o’clock on that beautiful, breezy autumn day when Mr. Casaubon drove away to his rectory at Lowick, just five miles from Tipton. Already wearing her bonnet and shawl, Dorothea hurried through the shrubbery and across the park to wander in the wood along its boundary. Her only visible companion was Monk, the great St. Bernard who always guarded the young ladies on their walks. A girl’s vision of a possible future had opened before her. She looked towards it with trembling hope and wanted to roam through it uninterrupted. She walked briskly in the brisk air, colour rising in her cheeks, and her straw bonnet slipped slightly backwards—a bonnet our contemporaries might examine with puzzled curiosity, like an obsolete kind of basket. Her portrait would perhaps be incomplete without mentioning that she wore her brown hair in flat braids coiled behind her head, daringly exposing its shape at a time when public taste demanded that nature’s scantiness be disguised with high barricades of frizzed curls and bows, surpassed by no great people except the Fijians. This was one sign of Miss Brooke’s asceticism. Yet nothing ascetic showed in her bright, full eyes as she looked ahead, not consciously observing but drawing into her intense mood the afternoon’s solemn splendour: its long swathes of light between distant rows of lime trees whose shadows met.

Anyone, young or old—anyone, that is, in those days before Reform—would have found her an appealing sight if they had attributed the glow in her eyes and cheeks to the ordinary images of newly awakened young love. Poetry has given ample consecration to Chloe’s illusions about Strephon, as it should to the touching beauty of all spontaneous trust. Miss Pippin adoring young Pumpkin, dreaming down endless avenues of tireless companionship, was a little drama our fathers and mothers never tired of, and it had been dressed in every costume. Let Pumpkin merely possess a figure that could survive the disadvantages of a short-waisted tailcoat, and everyone thought it not only natural but necessary to perfect womanhood that a sweet girl should instantly believe in his virtue, his exceptional abilities and, above all, his absolute sincerity. Yet perhaps nobody then alive—certainly nobody near Tipton—could have sympathized with a girl whose dreams of marriage took their colour entirely from an exalted enthusiasm for life’s purposes. That enthusiasm burned chiefly on its own fuel and took no account of the details of bridal clothing, the pattern of silverware, or even the honours and tender pleasures of a flourishing married woman.

Dorothea had now begun to think Mr. Casaubon might want her for his wife, and the possibility filled her with a kind of reverent gratitude. How good of him—indeed, it would be almost like a winged messenger suddenly appearing beside her path and extending his hand! For a long time uncertainty had oppressed her, hanging like thick summer haze over her desire to make her life greatly useful. What could she do, what should she do? She was barely more than a girl, yet had an active conscience and a great intellectual hunger that could not be fed by the education offered to girls, with its nibbles and judgments like those of a wandering mouse. Had she possessed a little more stupidity and conceit, she might have thought a wealthy Christian young lady’s ideal life lay in village charities, patronizing the poorer clergy, and reading “Female Scripture Characters,” with its revelations of Sara’s private experience under the Old Dispensation and Dorcas’s under the New. She might have tended her soul over her embroidery in her own sitting room, with marriage in the background to a man less strict than herself—men being involved in affairs religion could not explain—whom she could pray for and advise at suitable moments. Poor Dorothea was excluded from such contentment. The intensity of her religious nature and the power it exerted over her life were only one aspect of a temperament wholly passionate, theoretical and intellectually consistent. Such a nature, struggling in the bonds of a narrow education and enclosed by a social life that seemed merely a maze of petty pursuits, a walled labyrinth of small paths leading nowhere, was bound to appear both excessive and inconsistent to others. Whatever seemed best to her, she wanted to justify with the fullest knowledge, rather than live in a pretended acceptance of rules nobody followed. All her youthful passion still poured into this hunger of the soul. The union that attracted her would release her from a girl’s subjection to her own ignorance, giving her the freedom of willingly submitting to a guide who would lead her along the grandest road.

“Then I would learn everything,” she told herself, still walking quickly along the woodland bridleway. “It would be my duty to study, so I could help him better in his great work. Nothing in our lives would be trivial. Our everyday things would stand for the greatest things. It would be like marrying Pascal. I’d learn to recognize truth by the same light that great men have seen it by. Then, when I was older, I’d know what to do. I’d understand how to lead a great life here, now, in England. At present I can’t feel certain of doing good in any way. Everything is like going on a mission to people whose language I don’t speak—except building decent cottages. There can be no doubt about that. Oh, I hope I could get the people at Lowick properly housed! I’ll draw plenty of plans while I have the time.”

Dorothea stopped her thoughts abruptly, reproaching herself for so presumptuously counting on uncertain events. But the appearance of a rider cantering round a bend spared her any inward effort to change their course. The well-groomed chestnut and two handsome setters left no doubt that it was Sir James Chettam. Seeing Dorothea, he dismounted at once, handed his horse to his groom and approached her carrying something white on his arm, at which the two setters barked excitedly.
“How delightful to meet you, Miss Brooke,” he said, lifting his hat to reveal smoothly waved fair hair. “It brings forward a pleasure I’d been looking forward to.”

Miss Brooke resented the interruption. This pleasant baronet, who really would make Celia a suitable husband, overestimated the need to please the older sister. Even a future brother-in-law can become oppressive if he constantly assumes too close an understanding and agrees with you even when you contradict him. The thought that he might mistakenly be courting her could not form: all her mental energy was occupied with convictions of another kind. At this moment he was positively intrusive, and his dimpled hands were quite disagreeable. Irritation made her flush deeply as she returned his greeting with some hauteur.
Sir James read her heightened colour in the way most flattering to himself, and thought he had never seen Miss Brooke look so lovely.

“I’ve brought a little petitioner,” he said, “or rather, I’ve brought him to see whether you approve before he makes his petition.” He displayed the white thing under his arm: a tiny Maltese puppy, one of nature’s most artless toys.
“It hurts me to see creatures bred solely to be pets,” Dorothea said. Her opinion was forming at that very instant, as opinions do, in the heat of irritation.
“Oh, why is that?” Sir James asked as they walked on.

“I don’t believe all the fondling makes them happy. They’re too helpless, their lives too fragile. A weasel or mouse that finds its own living is more interesting. I like to imagine the animals around us have souls something like ours, and either conduct their own little business or can be our companions, like Monk here. Those creatures are parasites.”
“I’m so glad to learn you don’t like them,” said the good Sir James. “I’d never keep one for myself, but ladies are usually fond of these Maltese dogs. Here, John, would you take this dog?”

Thus the objectionable puppy, with equally black and expressive nose and eyes, was disposed of, since Miss Brooke had decided it would have been better unborn. Still, she felt an explanation was needed.

“You mustn’t assume Celia feels as I do. I think she likes little pets. She once had a tiny terrier she loved dearly. It made me anxious because I was afraid I’d step on it. I’m rather short-sighted.”
“You have an opinion of your own about everything, Miss Brooke, and it’s invariably a good one.”
What could anyone say in reply to such foolish flattery?
“You know, I envy you that,” Sir James continued as they walked at the fairly brisk pace Dorothea had set.
“I’m not quite sure I understand your meaning.”
“Your ability to reach an opinion. I can judge people; I know when I like someone. But with other things, you know, I often find it hard to decide. You hear very sensible arguments on both sides.”
“Or arguments that sound sensible. Perhaps we don’t always distinguish sense from nonsense.”
Dorothea felt she was being rather discourteous.
“Exactly,” said Sir James. “But you seem able to make that distinction.”
“Quite the opposite: I often can’t decide. But that’s because I don’t know enough. The right answer still exists, even if I can’t see it.”

“I think few people would see it sooner. You know, Lovegood told me yesterday you had the best idea imaginable for a cottage plan—quite extraordinary in a young lady, he thought. You had real _genus_, as he put it. He said you wanted Mr. Brooke to build a new group of cottages, though he seemed to doubt your uncle would agree. Now, that’s something I want to do myself—on my own estate, I mean. I’d be delighted to put your plan into practice, if you’d let me see it. Of course, you don’t get your money back; that’s why people object. Labourers can never pay enough rent to make it profitable. Even so, it’s worth doing.”

“Worth doing! Yes, indeed,” Dorothea said passionately, forgetting her earlier petty irritations. “We deserve to be driven out of our lovely houses with a whip of small cords—all of us who let our tenants live in the pigsties we see around us. Life in a cottage could be happier than ours, if the cottages were proper homes fit for human beings from whom we expect duty and affection.”
“Would you let me look at your plan?”

“Yes, certainly. I’m sure it has plenty of faults. But I’ve studied all the cottage plans in Loudon’s book and selected what seemed best in them. Oh, how happy I’d be to set an example round here! I think instead of Lazarus at the gate, we should put those pigsty cottages outside the park gates.”

Dorothea was now in the happiest mood. Sir James as her brother-in-law, building model cottages on his estate; perhaps others built at Lowick, then more and more elsewhere in imitation—it would be as though Oberlin’s spirit had swept through the parishes and made poverty’s life beautiful!

Sir James examined all the plans and took one away to discuss with Lovegood. He also carried away a satisfied feeling that he was advancing rapidly in Miss Brooke’s esteem. The Maltese puppy was never offered to Celia. Dorothea later remembered this omission with surprise, but blamed herself: she had monopolized Sir James. Still, it was a relief to have no puppy underfoot.

Celia was there while the plans were studied, and noticed Sir James’s delusion. “He thinks Dodo cares for him, when she only cares for her plans. Yet I’m not sure she’d refuse him if she thought he’d let her direct everything and carry out all her ideas. And how uncomfortable Sir James would be! I can’t bear ideas.”

Indulging this dislike was Celia’s private luxury. She dared not state it outright to her sister, since that would invite a demonstration that she was somehow opposed to goodness itself. On safe occasions, however, she found indirect ways to bring her negative wisdom to bear on Dorothea. She could pull her sister out of rapture by reminding her that people were staring rather than listening. Celia was not impulsive. Whatever she wanted to say could wait, and it always emerged in the same quiet, evenly clipped manner. When others spoke with energy and emphasis, she merely watched their faces and features. She could never understand how well-bred people agreed to sing, opening their mouths in the absurd way that exercise required.

Within a few days Mr. Casaubon called one morning and was invited to dine and stay overnight the following week. Dorothea thus had three more conversations with him and became convinced her first impressions were correct. He was everything she had imagined. Almost every remark seemed a specimen brought up from a mine, or an inscription over a museum door that might open onto the treasures of past ages. Her faith in his intellectual riches grew deeper and worked more powerfully upon her affections because it was now clear he came to see her. This accomplished man stooped to notice a young girl and took the trouble to address her understanding, rather than offer foolish compliments, sometimes even correcting her instructively. What delightful companionship! Mr. Casaubon seemed unaware that trivial matters existed. He never passed round the small talk of ponderous men, as welcome as stale wedding cake smelling of the cupboard. He spoke about what interested him or kept silent, bowing with melancholy courtesy. Dorothea found this adorably genuine: a religious refusal of the artificiality that exhausts the soul in pretence. She revered his spiritual superiority to her as much as his intellect and scholarship. He agreed with her expressions of devotion, usually supplying a fitting quotation. He permitted himself to mention spiritual struggles in his youth. In short, Dorothea believed she could count on understanding, sympathy and guidance here. On one subject—just one—dear to her, she was disappointed. Mr. Casaubon apparently took no interest in building cottages. He turned the conversation towards the extremely cramped homes of the ancient Egyptians, as if to discourage excessively high standards. After he left, his indifference troubled her. Her mind busied itself with arguments about differences of climate that change human needs, and the acknowledged wickedness of pagan despots. Shouldn’t she put these arguments to him next time? Further reflection, however, told her she was presumptuous to claim his attention for such a topic. He would not object to her pursuing it in spare moments, as other women expected to occupy themselves with clothes and embroidery; he would not forbid it when—Dorothea felt rather ashamed to catch herself speculating like this. But her uncle had been invited to spend a couple of days at Lowick. Was it reasonable to suppose Mr. Casaubon enjoyed Mr. Brooke’s company for its own sake, with or without documents?

Meanwhile that small disappointment increased her pleasure in Sir James Chettam’s eagerness to begin the improvements she wanted. He visited much more often than Mr. Casaubon, and she stopped finding him disagreeable once he proved so thoroughly serious. He had already applied considerable practical ability to Lovegood’s estimates, and was charmingly willing to follow her lead. She suggested building two cottages and moving two families out of their old hovels, which could then be demolished and replaced on the same sites. Sir James said “Exactly,” and she tolerated the word remarkably well.

Certainly men with so few ideas of their own could be very useful members of society under sound feminine guidance—provided they chose their sisters-in-law well! It is hard to say whether she was being a little wilful in remaining blind to the possibility that a different kind of choice concerning her was at stake. Just now, however, her life overflowed with hope and activity. Besides considering her plans, she took learned books from the library and hurried through many subjects so that she might be a little less ignorant in conversation with Mr. Casaubon. All the while her conscience kept asking whether she was overvaluing these poor efforts and viewing them with that self-satisfaction which is the final doom of ignorance and folly.
